name: Nora Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead eight buyers for a large hotel company. At six each morning the kitchens send what arrived, what spoiled and what breakfast will run short of, and I call suppliers before the guests see an empty tray. I have an MBA and am one of the strongest people here at untangling a failed delivery, but I have never used an AI tool. I keep a paper list beside the order screen because I can see who has called back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does home look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and live with my partner Ivo, a bus driver, and our children, seven and thirteen. We have a mortgage. My senior post pays less than similar management jobs, but there are few of those jobs near us; Ivo's shifts help but do not cover every bill. A car engine replacement left us about two weeks of expenses in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the software stays small, our hotel kitchens still need someone to count the linen and food against the invoices. The company has stopped paying weekend cover at two sites because bookings are down. I feel that missing money every month, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my eight purchasing staff to keep the delivery tickets stapled to the invoice. I'd tell my manager the weekend-cover cut is putting late loads on weekday staff. I would not announce a new system to the cooks just because a vendor sent a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know every supplier who has missed a breakfast delivery in the last decade, and I run this team well. I have an MBA but the pay is low for a senior manager here. We have two weeks of expenses saved after our car engine failed, and only a few similar offices are close enough to keep the children in their schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Monday I'll check the last eight late breakfast loads with the kitchen leads and correct the delivery log. I'll ask payroll to show what the lost weekend cover took from my wage, then keep my ordinary schedule if the pay still covers mortgage and food. We will hold off on replacing the old sofa until we have a full month of expenses in cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. A normal week with no extra cover barely pays the bills, and the car already emptied our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why were you working weekend cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two hotels shared one buyer on weekends, and I handled the calls when something failed to arrive. The company moved those calls into weekdays, so I lost the paid cover. Breakfast trays still arrive at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would the sofa have cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 600, which is almost our whole cash reserve now. Our seven-year-old has drawn on it, but a marked sofa can wait. The mortgage cannot wait for a clean sofa.

I'd tell the cooks we still need **delivery tickets** beside invoices.
think: My **lower manager pay** leaves little room to rebuild cash after the car repair.
With **two weeks saved**, few nearby offices let our children stay in their schools.
do: Check **eight late breakfast loads** with kitchen leads on Monday.
Ask payroll to measure **lost weekend pay**.
Delay the **600 sofa** until cash reaches a month of expenses.
feel: I feel **anxious** about bills after the cover cut.
S0.quote: The mortgage cannot wait for a clean sofa.
fieldNote: Lost **weekend cover** is her current income problem even in a plateau.
Her MBA and supplier memory coexist with **low manager pay**.

Delay 600 sofa until cash reaches one month of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stronger system could write orders, check prices, plan menus and answer our hotel managers. Those are most of my team's hours, even though the cooks still handle food. It could make our eight-person desk a small exception desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kitchen leads to keep a named person for failed cold deliveries. I'd ask the company for a paid trial on old invoices and a clear count of posts before changing the rota. I would say I have never used AI and need somebody to explain exactly what it will do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my team may fall from eight to four and my senior role could be folded into another region. I have earned trust by knowing which supplier can deliver before dawn, but that knowledge is in our records too. A second salary from Ivo's bus driving covers part of the mortgage, not our full monthly costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask our finance lead to show me ten old disputed invoices in the proposed tool, with paid time and a colleague beside me if the director approves a trial. I'd keep the current delivery phone line while the tool is tested, and ask for written staffing numbers before a live rollout. If a posted food-service manager job appears locally, I'd apply only after checking its wage and hours; I would leave this wage only for a signed offer covering mortgage, food and the children's costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious and a little embarrassed at needing a lesson on a screen. I will take it if the trial is real, but the company cannot call a demonstration a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the tool on live orders?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not until the finance lead proves the old invoice checks and the director approves it. I do not want an untrained click sending fifty breakfast boxes to the wrong hotel. My staff can show me, but they must be paid for that time too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ivo at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the manager job may be merged, and his driving pay cannot fill the gap. I would bring home the written headcount plan if there is one. I don't want our thirteen-year-old hearing it from a worried colleague's child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 full AGI could place orders, resolve invoices and plan breakfast stocks for every hotel. It could do my desk and even the alternative manager desk I might apply for. The kitchen still needs people carrying and preparing food until capable robots arrive around 2031, but I do not have a cook's certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my staff to ask for notice terms and actual paid kitchen vacancies, not just courses. I'd tell Ivo we should cancel the sofa and the planned holiday deposit now. I'd tell the cooks that I won't claim their jobs are safe after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the purchasing desk and my manager wage to go. Ivo's bus pay is real, but it won't cover mortgage, groceries and two children; two weeks saved would vanish after one missed salary. I would be awake listening for the next bill notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the kitchen director whether there is a posted paid food-preparation trainee place and what hygiene certificate it needs. I'd apply for the certificate only if the company funds it on paid time, the kitchen can supervise me and Ivo or another agreed adult covers school pickup. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I'd take a posted kitchen job only if its wage with Ivo's confirmed pay covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd ask the lender about hardship terms before arrears and check public help eligibility before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I know the breakfast orders. Knowing a breakfast order is not the same as preparing fifty meals for pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the children in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They will be nine and fifteen. I won't tell them the mortgage is their problem, but I would say the holiday is paused. The younger one still needs somebody at pickup when both adults work early shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the kitchen place last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chopping and carrying might pay until robots can do those tasks around 2031. Menu planning, stock levels and ordering would face AGI in 2028. A three-year physical opening is worth checking, but it is not a guarantee of years of wages.

I'd tell Ivo the **holiday deposit** must wait while we check wages.
think: I expect my **manager wage to end** by 2028.
Ivo's bus pay and two weeks cash cannot cover **our family costs**.

Take **posted kitchen work** after 2028 only if combined confirmed wages cover bills.

feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely lost wage and two weeks cash.

fieldNote: She distinguishes **purchasing expertise** from safe paid kitchen preparation.
Her kitchen idea needs **funding, supervision and pickup** before any course.
Food preparation is physical until **2031 robots**, while ordering faces AGI in 2028.

steps.text: Apply for company-funded hygiene certificate only on paid time with supervision and agreed pickup
Take posted paid kitchen job only if confirmed combined wages cover mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years could let me learn whether I can work safely in a kitchen before my desk is at risk in 2031. Full AGI would still take purchasing and menu planning then. The lifting and cooking could keep people employed until capable robots arrive around 2034, if the company keeps those posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to post trainee wages and shift times next to any course. I'd tell Ivo that the current mortgage must be paid before we promise extra savings. I'd ask the kitchen leads to tell me plainly whether I can keep up on a breakfast shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be able to move from ordering to the breakfast line, but I would start as a beginner despite being good at management. The lower trainee wage may be impossible for our mortgage. With five years I can test it on paid time instead of resigning for an idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd request two paid supervised breakfast shifts per month and complete them only if the kitchen director approves, hygiene instruction is completed, my office shift is covered and Ivo agrees to pickup. I'd save 25 weekly if our regular wages cover mortgage, food and school costs, aiming for one month of expenses first. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted kitchen job only if its wage plus Ivo's confirmed pay covers those bills; if not, I'd keep looking for paid work and ask the lender for terms before missing a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious. I have time to measure a real shift and a real wage, but our cash is still thin today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the breakfast line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wash and prepare ingredients, check food temperatures with a trained cook and help move trays. I would not supervise cooking just because I supervised a purchasing team. A clean spreadsheet never kept soup at a safe temperature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ivo cannot do pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask another agreed adult and check the hours before accepting the shifts. If nobody can collect the younger child, I would not take that training slot. We cannot pay for childcare from a trainee wage we have not seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I will be 53, and our children will be seventeen and twenty-three. The younger may still have school costs; I don't know the older one's wages or plans. Purchasing decisions face AGI in 2036 and kitchen hands face capable robots around 2039, so I cannot sell myself a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager for a dated pay review now, with the weekend-cover loss in writing. I'd tell the family we can review the mortgage once a year and rebuild cash before buying the sofa. I'd tell the cooks I want real paid practice, not a ceremonial tour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could give us a smaller mortgage and more savings if our wages hold, although the low manager pay makes that slow. I would rather know by 2028 whether the kitchen suits me than wait for a 2036 layoff email. I still think the desk could go in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd ask for a written salary review tied to the extra hotels my team now covers, and look at the actual payroll result before changing our budget. I'd transfer 35 weekly to cash only while Ivo's shifts and my wage cover mortgage, food and school costs, aiming for three months of expenses without promising when. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd accept a posted paid kitchen role only if I have completed approved hygiene training, its wage with Ivo's confirmed pay covers bills and the younger child's travel or pickup is arranged; otherwise I'd keep searching paid work and ask the lender for terms early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin reserve, though a decade gives me a chance to improve it. A long runway is useful only if our pay reaches the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your older child help with the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope our older child is building an independent life at twenty-three. I do not know where they will live or what they will earn. I will not put an imaginary adult-child payment in the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pay review is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 35 weekly transfer would still depend on bills and Ivo's shifts; I would reduce or stop it if the money is not there. I would keep the old sofa and ask for posted paid shifts rather than take an unfunded course. Our kitchen table is where the numbers have to work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my manager wage to go before we have enough saved for even one mortgage month. A paid kitchen trial, an actual posted job with a wage we can live on and clear notice terms would help. I would need the younger child's pickup solved before an early kitchen shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the breakfast ready when a perfect order arrives but the milk is warm. A clean spreadsheet never kept soup at a safe temperature. The kitchen has its own skills, and I won't borrow them just because I know the invoice.

headlineQuote: The kitchen has its own skills, and I won't borrow them just because I know the invoice.
portrait: Nora, **43**, leads eight hotel buyers and holds an MBA, with strong supplier judgment and no AI use.
Her **low manager pay** and lost weekend cover strain a mortgaged household with two school-age children.
Ivo drives buses; a car repair left only **two weeks cash**, and few comparable offices are nearby.
She would test **paid kitchen work** under supervision but needs an actual wage, safe training and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her manager wage before a full mortgage month is saved.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **paid kitchen practice** and a posted job whose wage covers family bills.
She needs **clear notice terms** and a plan for the younger child's pickup.
